Aside from the moral outrage, this can be seen as an interesting sociological experiment in which most of Voats active userbase has taken part. I had my suspicions from the start because I began seeing posts from the same users on the same subject matter. Even after seeing his original post which admitted to the whole thing, I still saw the same old users submitting their claims that @she was at fault. What is more interesting is that I began seeing new users (who had never taken part in the drama) begin to express outrage over the fact that @she had not been removed.

Regardless of the intentions of @ElectroLumus, this was a sociological experiment which demonstrated the power a small group of people can have over a larger group of people. It was an elaborate chess game in which one side successfully predicted the actions of their opponent before the opposing move had been made. Politics is easy at a smaller level, it just goes by different names. In this case, Voats ruleset allowed for this behavior to successfully cause a witch hunt regardless of the targets guilt.

I have little doubt that the movement against @she will continue even after the comment by @ElectroLumus gains further traction. The herd mentality is strong in multi-communities like this. It happened in Digg, it happened in Reddit, and it happened here. The only thing that changed was the spectrum of the group mindset. For provocation to be successful, early attacks must be carefully crafted in order to get unwitting users to participate in the provocation itself, leading to a decentralized attack and making it difficult to ascertain the initial source and the validity of the initial attack. If successful, the initial source doesn't even need to continue its attack as the newly created decentralized network will continue the attack for the initial source. I may be an IT professional but I can recognize a botnet in any form.

There is one thing I disagree here and that is that the mods are not entirely to blame here. Both the mods and the users share similar attributes which are inherently flawed. That flaw is that they are human. I feel moderation is required but in order to successfully keep a community functioning a human touch is required. The trick is to be completely without bias, agenda, or opinion on either one of the two sides. If the mods have zero opinion and function as a human robot, then there is less chance that they will become successful targets for a small group of provocateurs. If the users lack opinion then there can be no witch hunt as provocateurs cannot function without a group to enrage (obviously this is unrealistic). It could be possible for bot to apply moderation rules set by the majority but this has two flaws:

  1. The rules which are set can be influenced by a small yet organized group

  2. Robots are not perfect

In the case of internet forums of this type, it can be understood that the flaw is inherent to the structure. If you had an AI capable of moderation then it could be possible to remove humans from moderation, assuming that the AI itself lacks opinions but can still distinguish between the nuances of opinion vs intentional provocation. None-the-less, no one would be able to believe that an AI has an axe to grind on a particular subject matter. Granted, this is just spitballing here. I would assume that the only realistic solution to this particular type of forum system is to have all moderators replaced by dull people who have no opinion and who will not post anything except moderation announcements. Finding such people is almost impossible in this day and age. Perhaps an IRS employee or maybe someone from the DMV.

Another option would be to remove common or popular subverses but that isn't remedying the problem but rather removing the option for such problems to occur in the first place. Even then, this could still happen but on a smaller scale. Past this, a committee of randomly selected users would be another solution, provided of course that the pool used was of active users and of a large enough sample that provocation would not come from inside potential provocateurs. These solutions are not my forte, however, as this is starting to really get into the theoretical political spectrum of knowledge.

As always, it's just my two cents on the matter. I'm quite sure there will be some differing opinions on this.

I was in my office about 3 blocks away from the world trade center. We heard a huge boom, and found out the first tower was hit. a little later, we heard a second boom and lost most communication with the outside world. So, at this point it was apparent we were under attack, and I had to vacate my office because it was in the next largest building in downtown Manhattan and possibly the next target based on it's proximity to the NYSE and the New York Federal Reserve. So .. out into the street where I thought it would be safer.

Since communications were down, we had no idea what was going on outside the area.

When the first building collapsed I was on Wall Street. I was the only one on Wall Street. and with the white clouds of "stuff" it looked like stock broker heaven. It was kind of surreal for a few minutes. Like everything slowed down. When I made my way to Broadway, everything sped up again. Anyway, I was one of those people wearing a dark suit covered with ash and blood that you saw on the news. I'm not sure where the blood came from. When the second building collapsed I made a beeline to Water Street amd walked uptown.

I lived way out in Queens, so I had to walk from the financial district to the Midtown tunnel in Manhattan, on 34th street. The police were trying to evacuate the city, so they were pulling drivers over and making them take "walkers" through the tunnel to Queens. I ended up with a family that dropped me off on the Long Island Expressway on the other side of the tunnel.

I hitch hiked and a guy headed to my neighborhood ended up picking me up (lucky I suppose). We sat in traffic for hours. It took me a nearly a full day to get home.

At home I threw out the suit and bloody shirt and changed into a pair of shorts and a t-shirt. To get my mind off things, I went to the driving range and wacked a few buckets of golf balls.

EDIT: a quick story .. The company I worked for at the time was AIG. A lot of my work with with the treasury group. Most of us working in downtown knew colleagues and had friends in the towers. It's a small community of wall street'ers and we tend to shift from bank to bank .. basically you can play 6 degrees with bankers and insurance folks. Anyway .. we were under attack and a woman from the treasury group at AIG had a husband that worked at the WTC. After the planes ran into the towers she was unable to get in touch with him. She was crying, thinking the worst, and her manager said ..hey sally, I know this is a really difficult time .. but we have to remember the important things here. We need to get these reports out before noon.

The manager get in loads of trouble and eveutually had to leave the company, and Sally's husband was OK .. just another fun 9/11 story

EDIT2 - also, to me this wasn't some traumatic experience. I'm not scarred for life or anything and I don't have PTSD - I'm good at dealing with things. It was a crappy thing that happened though, and i lost a few friends and a lot of colleagues that day. For that it sucked. I was able to help a number of less able people get to midtown, and what impressed me the most was how we Americans - from everywhere, pulled together to help one another. I don't think this is unique to NYC, I think that people everywhere would react the same way in an adverse situation. People at their core are generally good.

Dogecoin Core 1.10 Beta 1

Dogecoin 1.10 is a complete rebuild based on Bitcoin 0.11. This means in terms of the code-base we introduced all the changes between Bitcoin 0.9 and 0.11 into this version of Dogecoin Core.
We therefore suggest to read the release notes of both Bitcoin 0.10 and Bitcoin 0.11

Upgrading

To upgrade from any version below 1.10 you will need to re-index once, as the block database format has changed. If you run the Qt GUI client, it will prompt you to do so on the first start after the update. If you run a dogecoind daemon, you will need to start it with the parameter -reindex once after you updated. This process can take a few hours, depending on the performance of your machine.

Mining

For this beta release, we decided to disable AuxPoW mining, while further testing is completed. The functionality will be re-enabled in a later release candidate. EDIT: This does not mean we turned off AuxPoW. Just that mining is not possible with this version of the client ;) It will work just like before for everyone else, so this is solely of interest for pool admins.

Notable changes

For further explanation of these, see the above mentioned Bitcoin release notes.

Faster synchronization

Dogecoin Core 1.10 introduces headers-first and parallel block synchronization to greatly reduce the initial blockchain synchronization time.

Watch only address support

It is now possible to add public keys to your wallet that will be held in a "watch only" state. This means you will get information about incoming/outgoing transactions and resulting balance changes. Especially useful to keep track of your paper wallets.

Strict signature encoding (BIP66)

One of the reasons why mining is disabled on this release is the introduction of BIP66 which enforces strict rules about how transaction signatures are encoded and therefore will introduce a new block version (3). These rules will only activate once a certain number of blocks are mined with this new version. To not let this happen too early, mining is disabled for now. NOTE: This is not a hard fork, as all existing wallets will accept version 3 blocks, although they'll fail to enforce the new requirements.

Block file pruning

It is possible to run a Dogecoin node without keeping the full blockchain on your disk. This is currently incompatible with having a wallet on that client due to the fact that some actions regarding a wallet require the full block data. The minimum amount of kept blocks has been changed from Bitcoin to reflect our shorter block times.

General comments

Please backup your wallet regularly and especially before performing this upgrade. Do not copy your wallet.dat while Dogecoin Core is open. Instead you should either use the backup feature you find in the "File" menu or shut down Dogecoin Core completely before you make a copy of your wallet.dat.

Download

You can find all downloads here: https://github.com/dogecoin/dogecoin/releases/tag/v1.10-beta-1

Please let us know about any bugs you find. Either here or on GitHub :)
Thanks everyone for their continued support!

So... did anyone here actually read the New Yorker article they pulled this one quote from? The headline on techdirt seems to me like a gross misrepresentation of the overall tone of the article. Here's the final paragraph of the New Yorker story:

When government officials tell a private corporation to allow citizens to speak, are they upholding the First Amendment or flouting it? That was the question that President Reagan considered in 1987, when Congress moved to enshrine the fairness doctrine, arguing that it was necessary to “ensure the widest possible dissemination of information from diverse and antagonistic sources.” Reagan vetoed the bill, and delivered a stern statement explaining why. He said that government had no business telling radio and television stations what kinds of political discussions they should broadcast. Any effort in that direction would be “antagonistic to the freedom of expression guaranteed by the First Amendment.” In his view, robust debate was important—but free speech was more important still.

The article seems to address pros and cons of both sides of the argument, and seems to conclude that the preservation of free speech is of paramount importance.

techdirt seemingly takes a single sentence from the article and spins a narrative that the whole new yorker article must be about this one sentence:

And, just as good-faith gun-rights advocates don’t pretend that every gun owner is a third-generation hunter, free-speech advocates need not pretend that every provocative utterance is a valuable contribution to a robust debate, or that it is impossible to make any distinctions between various kinds of speech

And yes, techdirt is correct in pointing out that not all free-speech advocates pretend everything said is a valuable contribution to a debate, but this one single sentence does not invalidate the entirety of the article. To me, techdirt seems guilty of what they accuse the New Yorker of doing: making a broad, inaccurate generalization to reinforce a particular viewpoint. If you read both articles, it seems like the New Yorker does a much better job at taking a balanced approach whereas techdirt's language betrays their strong preexisting bias.
